previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: John, a man with a history of hypertension and alcohol use disorder, was admitted after a heavy drinking episode involving a gallon of vodka, presenting with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. He reported forgetting and not picking up his medications after a recent discharge. On admission, his heart rate was elevated at 130s, and he was treated with IV and oral diltiazem, followed by the addition of metoprolol to achieve rate control under 100. His chest pain was attributed to chest wall tenderness and gastritis, with normal cardiac enzymes and a clear chest X-ray. He received diazepam per CIWA protocol for alcohol withdrawal prevention, along with thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. Abdominal pain resolved with supportive care. By discharge, he was stable, alert, and ambulatory, with a simplified medication regimen including Campral to support alcohol cessation. He planned to engage in outpatient treatment and was discharged home with follow-up instructions.

Conversation with the patient on ___ with attending MD, 2

at that time, pt reported that he understood that need further

that he wanted his health care team to help him and that he 
would stay in the hospital for further evaluation. He appeared 
to understand the risks and benefits and did at that time appear 
to have capacity and be agreeable to plan of care. Suggested to 
pt to ask to speak to MD or RN as soon as he becomes upset with 
something rather than wait to he is very angry and threatening

again threated to leave AMA. Pt expressed that he did not like 
his doctor. I informed the patient that I was sorry he felt that 
way, but was only trying to work up his complaints and ensure 
his safety and health. I offered the patient a chance to explain 
his concerns surround this statement, but he would not 
elucidate. During times of examination by myself and nursing, pt 
had a very angry appearing affect on his face to the point where 
one should consider his/her safety. In addition, pt would often 
mumble things under his breath during examination and would not 
discuss what he was saying. Explained to pt that he would be 
having PMIBI today, ___ and would need to be NPO until test is 
complete. Explained to patient again need for medical treatments

leaving if the test was not performed by 3pm, then stated that 
he was leaving at 3pm no matter what. ___ agreed to stay. 
However, immediately after PMIBI was complete, pt dressed 
himself, packed his bag, and pulled off tele, pulled out his IV 
and announced that he was leaving. Explained again to patient 
risks of leaving as above including death, pt appeared to 
express knowledge of these concerns. However, he stated that 
""its ok"". When it was stated to him that we would like him to 
stay for further eval and monitoring and that he may die. He 
stated ""I'm fine, no I won't"".  If pt returns to this hospital, 
a full psychiatry capacity evaluation should be performed and 
perhaps a section 35.
